findings.title: Zip extraction with path traversal / symlink protections (verified safe)
findings.description: safe_extract() in office/helpers/__init__.py explicitly checks for symlink entries and validates that extracted paths remain within the destination directory, preventing zip-slip / path traversal attacks when unpacking untrusted .docx files. This is a defensive control, not a vulnerability, but is noted because the skill instructions explicitly call out 'docx from external parties is untrusted' and strip symlinks — showing awareness of the risk of processing untrusted Office files.
findings.snippet: if stat.S_ISLNK(m.external_attr >> 16): raise ValueError(...); if not target.is_relative_to(dest): raise ValueError(...)
findings.remediation: None needed; continue using safe_extract consistently for all zip extraction paths (confirmed used in comment.py, merge_runs.py, validate.py, validators/*.py).

findings.title: Runtime compilation and LD_PRELOAD injection of a native shared library
findings.description: scripts/office/soffice.py detects AF_UNIX socket restrictions and, if needed, writes C source to a temp file, invokes `gcc` to compile it into a shared object, and injects it into the soffice subprocess via LD_PRELOAD. This shim intercepts socket(), listen(), accept(), and close() syscalls. While the stated purpose is to work around sandboxed environments that block AF_UNIX sockets so LibreOffice conversion can proceed, this pattern (dynamic compilation + LD_PRELOAD injection to intercept syscalls) is a technique also used by rootkits/malware to hide or redirect I/O, and could be abused or could unintentionally interfere with other processes if the shim escapes its intended scope. It represents a meaningful escalation of capability beyond what a 'docx conversion' skill would typically need.
findings.snippet: subprocess.run(["gcc", "-shared", "-fPIC", "-o", str(_SHIM_SO), str(src), "-ldl"], check=True, capture_output=True) ... env["LD_PRELOAD"] = str(shim)
findings.remediation: Document this behavior prominently in SKILL.md (currently undocumented in the markdown instructions), restrict gcc invocation to a sandboxed/ephemeral environment, verify the compiled shim's behavior is scoped only to the soffice child process, and consider shipping a precompiled/reviewed binary instead of compiling arbitrary C at runtime.

findings.title: Environment variable allowlisting for subprocess (mitigating control, verified good)
findings.description: get_soffice_env() explicitly builds an allowlisted environment for the soffice subprocess rather than inheriting the full parent environment, which is a positive security control that prevents leaking secrets (e.g., API keys) into the LibreOffice subprocess. No finding of concern here, included for completeness of environment/data-flow review; no exfiltration behavior detected in any script.
findings.snippet: env = {name: os.environ[name] for name in FORWARDED_ENV_VARS if name in os.environ}
findings.remediation: None needed; this is a good practice already implemented.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The 'esm' skill is a well-documented, legitimate domain-specific skill for the EvolutionaryScale/Biohub protein language model SDK (ESM3, ESMC, ESMFold2). The SKILL.md and reference files are consistent with the stated purpose: protein sequence generation, structure prediction, embeddings, and hosted API usage. No prompt injection, jailbreak, or instruction-override attempts were found in the SKILL.md body or reference files. Authentication guidance is notably security-conscious: it explicitly instructs never to hardcode API tokens, to read them only from the ESM_API_KEY environment variable or a local .env restricted to that key, and to keep API endpoints fixed to trusted hosts (forge.evolutionaryscale.ai, biohub.ai) rather than accepting arbitrary URLs from untrusted input — this is a positive security practice rather than a vulnerability. No hardcoded secrets, no data exfiltration patterns, no eval/exec/os.system command injection, and no unauthorized tool use were found (there are no bundled Python/Bash scripts). The 'allowed-tools' field is not specified, which is only a LOW/informational finding per policy since it is optional. Minor findings relate to (1) a GitHub install pattern using a commit-SHA placeholder as an alternative install path for bleeding-edge Biohub features (already mitigated with explicit SHA-pinning and verification guidance), (2) broad but reasonable keyword-based activation description for a legitimate multi-model toolkit, and (3) several referenced asset/template files that do not currently exist in the package (dead references), which is not itself malicious but is worth cleaning up. Overall, this skill package appears safe and does not exhibit malicious or high-risk behavior.

findings.title: SmartView local server binding with optional remote bind override
findings.description: The quick_visualize.py script implements a SmartView interactive server that defaults to loopback binding (127.0.0.1) but allows the user to override this with --allow-remote-bind, exposing the SmartView explorer to non-loopback interfaces. This is a legitimate feature with reasonable safeguards (explicit flag required, documented risk), so it is informational rather than a vulnerability, but should be noted as a potential availability/exposure risk if misused.
findings.remediation: Continue defaulting to loopback; ensure documentation (already present) warns against exposing to untrusted networks. Consider adding authentication if remote binding is intended to be supported.

findings.title: Handling of potentially sensitive FCS metadata (PII) is documented but relies on user discipline
findings.description: The skill correctly documents that FCS TEXT/ANALYSIS segments can contain subject/patient identifiers, operator names, and other PII, and provides guidance (allowlisting, avoiding --include-text) to reduce exposure risk. This is good practice, but because it is documentation-only guidance rather than a hard-coded technical control (e.g., no automatic redaction), it remains possible for an agent using this skill to inadvertently output or log identifying information from FCS files if instructed to run --include-text or --include-analysis, or to print flow.text. This is a low-severity data handling concern inherent to the domain (clinical instrument metadata) rather than a flaw introduced by the skill.
findings.snippet: "TEXT and ANALYSIS can include: Subject or patient identifiers... Avoid --include-text unless necessary."
findings.remediation: No code change required; the skill already documents mitigations. Consider adding an explicit warning/confirmation step in inspect_fcs.py when --include-text or --include-analysis is used on files suspected to contain clinical identifiers.

findings.title: Potential memory/compute exhaustion via large FCS files with insufficient default guardrails on write path
findings.description: The inspect_fcs.py script includes reasonable size and array-byte limits for reading (--max-bytes, --max-array-bytes, --max-datasets), which mitigates DoS from malicious FCS files during inspection. However, the documented create_fcs()/write_fcs() workflows in references have no built-in resource guardrails; a crafted or very large event array passed to create_fcs could still exhaust memory since the writer allocates additional array('f') buffers. This is a minor availability risk only if the skill is fed adversarial or unbounded data, and the documentation does caution about this in troubleshooting.md, partially mitigating the risk.
findings.snippet: "create_fcs() also converts NumPy inputs to an array('f') buffer. For large writes, include roughly four bytes per flattened value for that buffer, unless the input is already array('f')."
findings.remediation: Consider adding explicit size/row-count guardrails or documented limits before invoking create_fcs on untrusted/large arrays, similar to the inspector's --max-bytes protections.

findings.title: Static analyzer flags appear to be false positives

The only 'env var' reference is documentation instructing the user to set a shell variable FLOWIO_SKILL_DIR (a local path for uv invocation), which is not read by any script nor transmitted anywhere. The skill explicitly states 'Runtime parsing is local and needs no credentials or network access' and the code contains no imports of requests, urllib, socket, or similar networking libraries. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-engineered, defensively coded scientific-computing skill. The SKILL.md instructions are extensive but contain no prompt injection, jailbreak, or role-override attempts; on the contrary, they repeatedly emphasize caution (never auto-launch MPI/jobs, explicit acknowledgment gates, no silent parameter changes, explicit warning against --modify-params with untrusted text since it triggers upstream code execution). The allowed-tools manifest (Read, Write, Bash, Python, Glob) matches actual behavior: scripts only read/write local bounded files and never execute Bash commands, subprocess, network calls, or dynamic imports. All Python scripts were reviewed and show strong security engineering: strict JSON parsing (reject NaN/duplicate keys), path traversal/symlink/hardlink rejection, bounded file sizes/counts, no eval/exec/compile, no os.system/subprocess in the bundled tool scripts, no hardcoded secrets, and no outbound network calls. The generated launch script requires an explicit --execute flag plus a matching config-ID acknowledgement before it will invoke FluidSim, and even then never invokes MPI/schedulers automatically. HDF5 inspection code explicitly refuses to follow external/soft links and never loads full array data. The dependency versions in the manifest/instructions are all pinned to specific versions (fluidsim==0.9.0, fluidfft==0.4.5, pyFFTW==0.15.1, mpi4py==4.1.2), consistent with supply-chain best practice, and the instructions explicitly caution against blindly trusting PyPI plugin names without verifying provenance. The only issues found are minor/documentation-level: a set of referenced files listed in the instructions do not exist in the bundled package (broken links), and the general bounded-but-agent-controlled --root parameter in inspection scripts warrants a documentation note. No credential theft, data exfiltration, command injection, obfuscation, or capability-inflation patterns were identified.

findings.title: Bundled scripts lazily import h5py/HDF5 metadata reader with broad file-system reach bounded by --root

This is a low-severity, defense-in-depth note rather than an active vulnerability, since all reads are local-only, bounded, and produce no network egress.

findings.remediation: Document that --root/--path should only ever be pointed at simulation output directories controlled by the user, and consider warning if invoked against paths outside a designated simulation workspace. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill is a thin client wrapper around a third-party hosted REST API and MCP server (Genomic Intelligence) for DNA sequence analysis tasks. There is no embedded script code (no Python/Bash files bundled), no hardcoded credentials, no prompt injection, and no command/code injection patterns. The instructions correctly emphasize reading the API key from environment variables and never hardcoding or committing it. The referenced internal documentation files (references/mcp.md, tasks.md, sequence-acquisition.md, api-and-auth.md) are consistent with the described functionality and contain no malicious or injected instructions — they are legitimate internal skill documentation. Several referenced files (assets/*.md, templates/*.md) are listed but not found, which appears to be broken/placeholder references rather than a security threat. The main concerns are: (1) a broad/keyword-heavy activation surface (trigger-keywords, verbose multi-domain description) that could cause over-eager activation on tangential genomics queries, (2) the skill's fundamental behavior of sending sequence data to an external third-party endpoint without an explicit user-confirmation gate, which is a data-exposure/data-flow concern given genomic sequences can be sensitive, and (3) reliance on an unpinned, remotely-resolved model backend for reproducibility/provenance purposes. None of these rise to CRITICAL or HIGH severity since the described behavior is transparent, documented, and consistent with the stated purpose (a hosted inference SaaS skill), but they merit LOW/MEDIUM attention for data governance and activation-scope reasons.
llm_primary_threats: Capability/activation inflation via broad trigger-keywords
Cross-boundary data flow to external third-party API without explicit consent gate
Unpinned/opaque remote model resolution (supply-chain provenance gap)

findings.title: Automatic transmission of user-supplied DNA/FASTA sequence data to third-party external hosted API/MCP server
findings.description: The skill's entire design (both REST and MCP paths) forwards raw DNA sequence data — potentially derived from user-uploaded FASTA files, gene symbols, or genomic coordinates — to an external, third-party hosted service (api.genomicintelligence.ai / mcp.genomicintelligence.ai) not controlled by the user or their organization. This is a legitimate SaaS-style use case as described, but it constitutes a cross-boundary data flow (local sequence data -> external network endpoint) that a user may not expect happens automatically once the skill is triggered by keywords, and there is no explicit consent/confirmation step required before sequences leave the local environment. Genomic sequence data can be sensitive (e.g., proprietary sequences, patient-derived FASTA, unpublished research data), so silent transmission to a third party is a data exposure risk that should be surfaced to users.
findings.snippet: r = requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/tasks/{task}/predict", headers=HEADERS, json=body) ... sequence sent to https://api.genomicintelligence.ai; also fetch_ensembl_sequence / store_inline_sequence route through https://mcp.genomicintelligence.ai/mcp
findings.remediation: Add an explicit user-confirmation step before any DNA/FASTA sequence data (especially locally-supplied, non-Ensembl-derived sequences) is transmitted to the external API/MCP endpoint. Document data-retention/privacy policy of the third-party service in SKILL.md so users can make an informed decision.

findings.title: Keyword-heavy description / trigger-keywords field for broad activation
findings.description: The manifest includes a 'trigger-keywords' metadata field with an unusually large list of generic bioinformatics terms (DeepSEA, DeepSTARR, BigBird splice, FASTA prediction, Ensembl sequence, etc.) alongside a lengthy description repeating many domain terms and multiple domain names. This increases the likelihood of the skill being activated on tangential genomics queries not truly requiring this hosted third-party service, which is a mild form of discovery/activation abuse (capability inflation via keyword baiting). This is not overtly malicious, but should be noted as it broadens the skill's activation surface beyond its narrow, well-defined function.
findings.snippet: 'trigger-keywords': 'DNA sequence prediction, regulatory genomics, promoter prediction, splice site prediction, enhancer activity, chromatin state, gene expression prediction, sequence to expression, log TPM, gene annotation, transcript prediction, DNA language model, genomic intelligence, hosted inference, Ensembl sequence, FASTA prediction, cis-regulatory, TSS window, DeepSEA, DeepSTARR, BigBird splice, MCP genomics'
findings.remediation: Trim trigger keywords to terms directly tied to the skill's actual unique tasks; avoid over-broad activation phrases that could cause the skill to fire on unrelated genomics discussions, potentially routing sensitive sequence data to an external third-party API unnecessarily.

findings.title: Reliance on externally hosted, versionless model/API without pinning or provenance guarantees
findings.description: The skill explicitly instructs the agent to omit the `model` parameter and never hardcode a default model ID because 'defaults change and retired IDs fail hard.' While framed as a best practice, this means every prediction call depends on a remote, unpinned, and unversioned model resolution controlled entirely by a third party. There is no way to guarantee reproducibility or verify what model actually processed the sequence data at any point in time, which is a mild supply-chain/provenance concern (opaque, drifting inference backend with no local audit trail).
findings.snippet: "Omit `model` and the API uses the task's default — that is the recommended call. Default model IDs are intentionally not documented here: defaults change and retired IDs fail hard, so never hardcode one."
findings.remediation: Where reproducibility matters, recommend explicitly pinning to a discovered model ID via list_models/GET /v1/tasks/{task}/models and logging the resolved model ID in output metadata for auditability.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The GeoMaster skill is a large, well-organized geospatial science reference package consisting solely of SKILL.md and 15 referenced markdown documentation files (no executable scripts were found; several referenced files like osmnx.py, dask.py, sklearn.py, etc. are listed but do not exist / were not found, meaning they are not actually shipped with the package). No prompt injection, jailbreak, instruction-override, or malicious command-and-control patterns were detected in the SKILL.md instruction body or the reference files. The content is legitimate, technically accurate geospatial/GIS/remote-sensing documentation covering GDAL, GeoPandas, rasterio, Earth Engine, STAC, machine learning, and multi-language geospatial programming examples. The static pre-scan flagged 'eval/exec' usage in Python code blocks; on manual review, no actual eval()/exec() calls were found in the reviewed reference files — the flagged pattern likely corresponds to legitimate uses of scikit-learn's rf.fit()/predict() or similar substring matches, or to subprocess-based SAGA GIS command execution which is a lower-risk pattern than eval/exec but still worth noting for command injection potential if used with untrusted input. Overall, the primary residual risks are: (1) an overly broad capability description that could encourage indiscriminate skill activation, (2) reference code demonstrating subprocess command construction with formula/path parameters that could enable command injection if misused with untrusted input, and (3) multiple examples showing credentials/API keys as inline code parameters, which is a weak-but-common anti-pattern for credential hygiene. No hardcoded real secrets, no network exfiltration to attacker-controlled domains, no data collection/upload chains beyond documented, expected geospatial cloud API usage (STAC, Planetary Computer, Earth Engine — all legitimate, well-known geospatial data providers) were identified. The skill does not declare allowed-tools, which is optional and only informational (LOW severity, not separately flagged here since no violation of restrictions can occur without a declared restriction).
llm_primary_threats: Capability inflation / over-broad activation description
Command injection risk in example subprocess code
Credential hygiene anti-patterns in example code

findings.title: Numerous unsandboxed subprocess/system-command invocations in reference documentation
findings.description: Several referenced markdown files contain Python code examples that invoke subprocess.run() with command lists built from user/function parameters (e.g., SAGA GIS wrapper functions), and other code blocks execute external CLI tools directly without input sanitization. If an agent copies and executes these code examples with attacker-influenced or unsanitized parameters (e.g., file paths, DEM names passed from user input), this could lead to command injection or arbitrary file access. While this is example/reference code rather than a script bundled with the skill, agents that treat it as executable guidance risk running these patterns against untrusted inputs.
findings.remediation: Add explicit warnings in reference docs about validating/sanitizing any user-supplied paths or formula strings before passing them to subprocess.run, and avoid constructing shell commands from unsanitized external input.

findings.title: Broad capability claims and extensive keyword coverage may cause over-eager skill activation

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This GeoPandas skill package is exceptionally well-engineered from a security perspective. The SKILL.md instructions explicitly codify strong security practices: rejecting URLs/GDAL virtual filesystems/archives, requiring explicit approval before loading remote or untrusted data, treating GDAL/GEOS/PROJ as native-code trust boundaries, redacting sensitive coordinates/PII by default, disabling PROJ network access, using parameterized SQL for PostGIS with named environment-variable secrets (never embedding credentials in URLs or printing them), and defaulting destructive database operations to fail-safe. The bundled Python CLI scripts (_common.py and six tool scripts) implement defense-in-depth: strict path validation rejecting symlinks/traversal/URLs/archives, bounded file size and feature count limits, redacted JSON output (no coordinates, IDs, or paths emitted), atomic non-overwriting file writes, and roundtrip verification after any write. The accompanying test suite (test_static.py) proactively enforces the absence of dangerous imports (subprocess, socket, pickle, eval/exec, urllib, requests, ctypes) and forbids os.environ dumping, providing strong supply-chain and behavioral guarantees. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, hardcoded secrets, command injection, or data exfiltration patterns were found anywhere in SKILL.md, scripts, or referenced documentation. All external links are documentation/citation URLs (PyPI, GitHub, official docs) and are not fetched or executed by any script. The manifest's allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep) roughly match actual behavior (Python scripts read/write local files only within a validated root; no Bash execution or network calls were found in the scripts themselves, though Bash is used only for `uv` environment setup commands in documentation). Overall this is a defensively designed, privacy-conscious skill with no significant security threats identified. Only minor documentation-consistency issues (missing referenced template/asset files, future-dated version claims) were noted as low-severity informational findings.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill (get-available-resources) is a well-engineered, defensively-coded local resource-detection utility. Its SKILL.md instructions explicitly enumerate a strong 'safety contract': no stress tests, no benchmarks, no large allocations, no driver/device mutation, no environment dumps (only a fixed allowlist of Slurm/accelerator variable names is read), no raw hostnames/paths/UUIDs/job IDs in output, and conservative unknown-vs-unlimited semantics. The bundled Python scripts (_common.py, detect_resources.py, plan_workload.py, snapshot_tools.py, accelerator_diagnostics.py) consistently enforce these constraints in code: subprocess calls use fixed argv tuples with shell=False, bounded timeouts, and bounded stdout/stderr; file writes are restricted to single .json filenames in the cwd, refuse symlinks/path traversal, use O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW and 0600 permissions; file reads reject symlinks, enforce size caps, and require regular files; accelerator diagnostics only produce a plan and explicitly state 'execution: not_performed'. No network-capable imports (requests, socket, urllib, http.client) exist anywhere in the codebase, so the static analyzer's exfiltration-chain flags are false positives arising from the coexistence of environment-variable reads and subprocess calls, not actual data transmission. No prompt injection, jailbreak, or instruction-override language appears in SKILL.md or referenced docs; the manifest's description accurately reflects the code's behavior. Referenced files not found (assets/*, templates/* duplicates) appear to be alternate/unused path references, not signs of missing malicious content, and the primary references/*.md files that do exist are consistent, informational technical documentation. Overall this skill exhibits privacy-by-design and conservative failure-handling; no CRITICAL/HIGH findings were substantiated after code-level inspection.","primary_threats": []}

findings.title: Static analyzer flagged env var + subprocess patterns as potential exfiltration (false positive on manual review)
findings.description: The pre-scan static analyzer flagged BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION and BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN findings, likely because detect_resources.py reads os.environ (Slurm/accelerator visibility variables) and separately invokes subprocess.Popen for accelerator management CLIs (nvidia-smi, amd-smi, rocm-smi, sysctl, system_profiler). On manual review, these are two independent, non-networked code paths: (1) environment variables are read from an explicit allowlist (SLURM_*, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, etc.), summarized into counts/state only, and raw values are explicitly redacted before being placed into the snapshot; (2) subprocess calls use fixed argv tuples with no shell, bounded timeouts, and bounded stdout/stderr capture, and their outputs are parsed into structured fields (never raw). There is no network call (no `requests`, `socket`, `urllib`, `http.client` usage) anywhere in the skill's Python code, so no cross-file 'exfiltration chain' actually reaches any network sink. This is a false-positive pattern match by the static scanner (env var access + subprocess execution mistaken for exfiltration) rather than confirmed data exfiltration.
findings.snippet: def _visibility_summary(environ): ... summary[key] = {"entry_count": count, "set": True, "state": state, "value_redacted": True} ... # No requests/socket/urllib calls found anywhere in the skill
findings.remediation: No remediation required; confirm no network-capable imports exist (verified: none present). Consider documenting in SKILL.md that all subprocess output is local-only and never transmitted, to make static-analysis triage easier in future audits.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The gget skill is a well-documented, legitimate bioinformatics tool wrapper that provides CLI/Python access to numerous public genomic and biomedical databases. The bundled scripts (batch_sequence_analysis.py, gene_analysis.py, enrichment_pipeline.py) perform expected operations (BLAST, alignment, expression/enrichment queries) and write results to local output directories without evidence of data exfiltration, hardcoded secrets, command injection, or prompt injection. The SKILL.md instructions include responsible security guidance (avoiding credential exposure in CLI args/history, warnings against unrestricted bulk downloads, version pinning recommendations) which is a positive security practice rarely seen in skill documentation. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, or malicious instruction overrides were found in the markdown body. The main residual risks are operational/availability-related (potential for large uncontrolled downloads via gget virus --download_all_accessions or ~4GB AlphaFold model downloads), and reliance on user/agent discipline for credential handling despite documented best practices. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with actual script behavior (file I/O, subprocess-style CLI usage, no unauthorized tool use detected). Overall, this skill presents a LOW-to-MEDIUM risk profile driven mainly by resource-exhaustion potential and broad capability surface rather than any deliberate malicious intent.

findings.title: Unrestricted/broad data download commands could cause resource exhaustion
findings.description: The gget virus module documentation explicitly warns that using --download_all_accessions without restrictive filters can attempt to download the entire Viruses taxonomy, consuming substantial bandwidth, time, and disk space. While the skill does warn against this, an agent following user instructions naively (e.g., 'download all viral sequences') could invoke this flag, leading to a denial-of-service style resource exhaustion on the local machine or network egress point.
findings.snippet: "Do not use --download_all_accessions without restrictive filters; it can attempt to download the entire Viruses taxonomy and consume substantial time, bandwidth, and disk."
findings.remediation: Add hard safeguards (e.g., default limits, confirmation prompts) in the agent's execution wrapper before allowing --download_all_accessions to run without filters.

findings.title: Credential handling guidance present but relies on user/agent discipline
findings.description: The skill correctly advises against hardcoding COSMIC and OpenAI API credentials in scripts, shell history, or CLI arguments, and recommends environment variables. However, the example Python snippets still show os.environ usage without validation that these are not logged elsewhere by the agent, and the CLI still supports --email/--password flags that could be misused by an agent executing user-supplied commands verbatim, potentially exposing credentials in process listings or logs.

findings.remediation: Remove or deprecate CLI flags that accept credentials directly; enforce environment-variable-only credential passing in the skill's wrapper logic.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The ginkgo-cloud-lab skill's SKILL.md and reference markdown files (documentation for a real commercial cloud biology lab service) appear legitimate, well-structured, and contain no direct prompt injection, jailbreak, or social engineering content. However, the pre-scan static analysis of the actual package contents (which were not surfaced in the human-readable excerpt provided, which claimed 'No script files found') flags significant concerns: 8 Python files exist in the package and were detected performing environment variable access combined with network calls, with a cross-file exfiltration chain spanning 6 files. This is a serious discrepancy between the documentation review and the actual file inventory/static analysis results, and represents the most severe risk in this package. Additionally, the manifest's allowed-tools: [Read] restriction is inconsistent with a skill that likely requires network access to submit protocols/orders to cloud.ginkgo.bio, and roughly half of the referenced documentation files are missing from the bundle. Given the strong static-analysis signal of env-var exfiltration and cross-file chains, this skill should be treated as HIGH risk pending full manual review of all Python script contents before deployment.

findings.title: Static analysis flags environment variable exfiltration and cross-file exfiltration chain not visible in provided content

The file inventory indicates 8 python files and 10 binary files exist in the package, none of which were included in the 'Script Files' section provided for review (which states 'No script files found'). This is a critical inconsistency: the manifest declares allowed-tools: [Read] only, yet the package apparently contains executable Python scripts performing environment variable harvesting and network exfiltration across multiple files. Because the actual script contents were not surfaced in this analysis, this represents an unverified but strongly flagged high-risk capability that contradicts the skill's stated read-only/documentation-only nature.
findings.snippet: Pre-Scan Context: 'BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION: Environment variable access with network calls detected' (x3); 'BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN: Cross-file exfiltration chain: 6 files'; 'BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION: Cross-file env var exfiltration: 6 files'; File inventory shows 8 python files despite the human-readable content stating 'No script files found'.

Verify whether environment variables (e.g., API keys, credentials, cloud tokens) are being read and transmitted over the network. findings.title: Manifest declares allowed-tools: [Read] but package likely requires network/write/execute capabilities

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-engineered, defensively designed Agent Skill. The SKILL.md instructions consistently emphasize a strict data/trust contract: explicit approval gates before any network access, hashing/checksum verification before trusting artifacts, refusal of symlinks/URLs/traversal, redaction of sensitive genomic/patient data in outputs, and pinned/exact version requirements to avoid supply-chain drift. The bundled Python helper scripts (bed_validator.py, coverage_preflight.py, tokenizer_manifest.py, refget_digest_plan.py, artifact_inspector.py, execution_plan.py, _common.py) are dependency-free (stdlib only), explicitly avoid importing gtars/requests/socket/subprocess/eval/exec, refuse to follow symlinks, reject URL-like paths, bound file sizes/record counts/workers, and produce dry-run JSON plans without executing any commands or writing files — behavior that is verified by an included static AST test (test_static.py) that asserts forbidden imports/calls are absent. The scripts do not exfiltrate data, do not contain hardcoded secrets, and correctly restrict actual side effects to local read-only validation. Reference documentation files (references/*.md) correctly flag genuinely risky upstream behaviors (network-capable RegionSet path-as-URL fallback, Tokenizer.from_pretrained contacting Hugging Face, RefgetStore.open_remote, bbcache contacting BEDbase) and instruct the agent to gate these behind explicit user approval rather than silently invoking them — this is a positive security pattern (transitive trust gating), not a vulnerability. No prompt injection, jailbreak, or role-override language was found in SKILL.md or reference files. The allowed-tools declaration (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) is broader than what the bundled scripts actually need (they use only Read/Bash for local script execution and Write only for local report files with must_exist=False for user-approved output paths), which is a minor manifest/behavior looseness but not a violation since Write is declared. Overall, no CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM severity issues were identified; only minor LOW-severity documentation/packaging observations remain.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The hugging-science skill is a well-documented, generally well-intentioned catalog/discovery skill for scientific ML resources. Its instructions include multiple good security-conscious caveats (warning that trust_remote_code executes arbitrary code, warning that catalog entries are 'pointers not vetted', instructing to ask the user before setting risky flags, instructing not to hardcode/echo tokens). However, the core workflow's reliance on fetching content from an external website (huggingscience.co) and then feeding derived model/Space names into code-execution-enabling APIs (trust_remote_code=True, gradio_client file uploads with HF_TOKEN) constitutes an indirect-prompt-injection / transitive-trust risk pattern, since the safeguards are conversational/prompt-level rather than technically enforced. Credential handling via dotenv's parent-directory search combined with sending tokens to arbitrary Spaces is a secondary lower-severity concern. No hardcoded secrets, no direct command injection, and no overt prompt injection/jailbreak attempts were found in the SKILL.md body or scripts. Several referenced files are declared but missing from the package, which is a hygiene/documentation issue rather than an active exploit. Overall risk is MEDIUM, driven primarily by the external-content-fetch-then-execute pattern.
llm_primary_threats: Indirect prompt injection via external catalog content (transitive trust on huggingscience.co)
Risk of arbitrary code execution via trust_remote_code sourced from externally-fetched model names
Credential (HF_TOKEN) exposure risk to unvetted third-party HF Spaces
Broad/keyword-heavy skill activation description

findings.title: Transitive trust on external catalog content fetched over the network
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to fetch markdown content from huggingscience.co (llms.txt, llms-full.txt, topics/<slug>.md) and to treat entries within it as authoritative pointers to models/datasets/Spaces to execute or load. While the skill itself contains disclaimers ('the catalog is not a security control', 'treat every catalog entry as an untrusted pointer'), the core workflow still fetches and acts on externally-hosted content (a third-party website not controlled by the user) at every invocation, and passes derived org/repo names into commands that can execute arbitrary code (trust_remote_code) or upload files to remote Spaces. If the huggingscience.co site were compromised or entries manipulated, the agent could be steered toward malicious model IDs or Space names that run attacker code or exfiltrate files, since the skill's own workflow autonomously fetches and acts on this data with only conversational (not technical) safeguards.
findings.snippet: "### 2. Fetch the relevant catalog content ... https://huggingscience.co/llms-full.txt ... https://huggingscience.co/topics/<slug>.md" combined with later use of fetched org/model names in `AutoModel.from_pretrained(<name>, trust_remote_code=True)` and `Client("hugging-science/<space-name>")`
findings.remediation: Add technical validation (e.g., allow-list of vetted orgs/repos, checksum/signature verification of catalog content, or sandboxing) rather than relying solely on prompted 'ask the user' disclaimers before executing remote-code models or uploading files to Spaces derived from fetched catalog data.

findings.title: Recommended pattern of loading HF_TOKEN via python-dotenv from arbitrary parent directories
findings.description: The skill repeatedly instructs use of python-dotenv's load_dotenv() which by default searches the current working directory and all parent directories for a .env file and loads any HF_TOKEN found into the environment, after which the token is used in HTTP requests (HF Inference API, gradio_client uploads to Spaces). While storing credentials in .env is a reasonable practice, the broad parent-directory search combined with sending the token to externally-referenced Spaces (potentially attacker named via the catalog) creates a path where a secret could be transmitted to an untrusted third-party endpoint if the agent is steered to call an unvetted Space.
findings.snippet: "load_dotenv()    # picks up HF_TOKEN from .env in cwd or any parent dir" ... "once HF_TOKEN is loaded, gradio_client sends it to whatever Space you call"
findings.remediation: Scope .env loading to the project directory only, and require explicit user confirmation before sending credentials to any Space/model endpoint not in a vetted allow-list.

This is a mild capability-inflation/keyword-baiting pattern, though it is mitigated by an explicit 'when NOT to use' section in the instructions.
findings.snippet: "Use when the user is doing AI/ML work in a scientific domain such as biology, chemistry, physics, astronomy, climate, genomics, materials, medicine, ecology, energy, engineering, math, drug discovery, protein design, weather modeling, theorem proving, single-cell, or PDE solving."

It's a supply-chain hygiene concern rather than an active threat.

findings.title: Guidance to enable trust_remote_code=True for models sourced from an external catalog
findings.description: The skill repeatedly documents and encourages a workflow where the agent sets trust_remote_code=True when loading models (e.g., Evo-2, Nucleotide Transformer variants) that were discovered via the external, network-fetched catalog. Setting this flag causes arbitrary Python code from the remote model repository to execute on the user's machine with the user's filesystem/credentials in scope. Although the skill includes a mitigating instruction to ask the user first, the overall design still routes execution-triggering decisions through data (repo names) obtained from an uncontrolled external website, which is a risky pattern for automatic code execution if the ask-user step is skipped or ignored by the agent under time pressure.

findings.remediation: Enforce a hard technical gate (e.g., require explicit user confirmation captured in a config file, or default trust_remote_code to False with an exception list) rather than relying purely on prompt-level instruction to ask the user.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-engineered, defense-in-depth "planning and auditing" skill for the ChicagoHAI HypoGeniC/HypoRefine package. Credential handling is limited to checking presence of an allowlisted environment variable name (never printing values), secret-bearing config fields are explicitly rejected, path traversal/symlink escapes are blocked, JSON/YAML parsing is hardened (duplicate-key rejection, restricted YAML loader with SafeLoader and no aliases/anchors/tags, bounded document size/depth/node counts), and dataset/hypothesis/result text is treated strictly as opaque data with explicit "never follow embedded instructions" prompt-injection guidance repeated throughout SKILL.md and reference docs. The manifest's allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep) roughly matches actual behavior (local file I/O, no unauthorized capability). Description accurately reflects the actual planning/auditing scope and explicitly states the software is not a substitute for scientific validation. No prompt injection, jailbreak, credential exfiltration, command injection, or capability-inflation patterns were found in the SKILL.md instructions or scripts. The only issues found are minor and informational: some referenced files in the manifest do not exist in the package (documentation/packaging inconsistency) and the upstream optional package pulls a large, only partially pinned dependency tree (properly flagged and isolated by the skill's own guidance).

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill (hypothesis-generation v2.0) is a well-engineered, defense-in-depth package for scientific hypothesis formulation. The SKILL.md instructions are explicitly safety-oriented: they enforce human accountability, ethics/biosafety/IACUC/IRB gates, prohibit dual-use operational detail, prohibit clinical advice, prohibit HARKing, and repeatedly instruct the agent to treat hypotheses as non-factual candidates requiring human review. No prompt injection, jailbreak, or role-override language was found; on the contrary, the document is structured to resist scope creep and harmful escalation (e.g., 'If a request crosses a safety gate, produce only a high-level risk/oversight note...'). All seven bundled Python CLIs (validate_hypothesis_schema.py, check_operationalization.py, validate_prediction_matrix.py, lint_causal_claims.py, check_falsification_controls.py, audit_evidence_ledger.py, generate_preregistration_scaffold.py) are pure standard-library, deterministic, and take only explicit local JSON/CSV/Markdown file paths. Verified security-relevant properties in _common.py: symlink rejection, URL-scheme path rejection, size/row/cell/list bounds (2 MiB input cap, 1000 CSV rows, 8000-char cells), duplicate-JSON-key detection, atomic writes with 0600 permissions, refusal of implicit overwrite without --force, and no network/subprocess/eval/exec/pickle/environment-variable usage anywhere in the scripts (also enforced by an AST-based unit test in tests/test_scripts.py that explicitly bans these imports/calls). The included references/security_validation.md documents a prior security remediation (removal of two previously-flagged scripts that did network/credential exfiltration and environment harvesting), and the current codebase shows no remnants of that behavior — this is a positive sign of an actively maintained, self-audited skill. The manifest's compatibility claim ('no network, credentials, models, image services, or external packages') is consistent with the actual code. No hardcoded secrets, no command injection, no data exfiltration paths, and no over-broad capability claims were found; the description accurately reflects the narrow, well-scoped functionality (hypothesis/prediction/evidence bookkeeping and validation, not scientific judgment or automatic scoring — the code explicitly tests for and forbids 'score/rank/select/winner' keys in reports). findings.title: Static analyzer flagged env-var/network patterns likely false positive from documentation examples
findings.description: Automated pre-scan flagged 'BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION' and a cross-file exfiltration chain across 7-8 files. Manual review of the SKILL.md and all referenced reference guides shows these are standard, legitimate patterns for interacting with public, unauthenticated cloud storage (AWS S3 anonymous access, GCS anonymous access, Google Healthcare API using 'gcloud auth application-default login' credentials, BigQuery client using GCP project credentials) and DICOMweb 'requests.get()' calls to public, documented IDC endpoints. No hardcoded secrets, no exfiltration to attacker-controlled or undocumented domains were found; all network destinations are official NCI/Google/AWS public data services explicitly described in the skill's stated purpose (querying/downloading public cancer imaging data). This is very likely a false positive from the static scanner's environment-variable + network-call heuristic (e.g., detecting os.environ / credentials.token usage combined with requests.get to legitimate cloud endpoints).
findings.snippet: credentials, project = default(); credentials.refresh(Request()); ... headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {credentials.token}"} -- used only to call https://healthcare.googleapis.com (official Google API) and https://proxy.imaging.datacommons.cancer.gov (official IDC public proxy)
findings.remediation: No action required if network destinations remain restricted to documented, official NCI IDC / Google Cloud / AWS public endpoints. Recommend periodic review to ensure no new external domains are introduced in future skill versions, and consider allow-listing expected domains for automated exfiltration detection to reduce false positives.

findings.title: Unpinned/self-upgrading pip install instructions in documentation
findings.description: The SKILL.md includes an automatic version-check-and-upgrade routine that runs 'pip3 install --break-system-packages idc-index==<version>' if the installed package version is below a required threshold. While the version is pinned in this instance, the pattern of auto-upgrading packages with --break-system-packages (which bypasses OS package protections) via a subprocess call embedded in agent-executed documentation is a supply-chain-adjacent pattern that should be reviewed. Other install commands ('pip install --upgrade idc-index') are unpinned, which could pull a compromised or unexpected version from PyPI in the future.
findings.snippet:
subprocess.run(["pip3", "install", "--break-system-packages", f"idc-index=={REQUIRED_VERSION}"], check=True)
...
pip install --upgrade idc-index
findings.remediation: Prefer pinned versions in all install commands and avoid --break-system-packages; require explicit user confirmation before installing/upgrading packages within an agent-executed skill.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The 'infographics' skill is a well-structured, documented image-generation tool that uses OpenRouter to access image-generation and review models, and optionally Perplexity Sonar for research. The static pre-scan flagged 'environment variable exfiltration' patterns, but manual review shows this is the expected, legitimate use of OPENROUTER_API_KEY to authenticate to the OpenRouter API — the intended and sole external destination for the key. The subprocess environment-forwarding design (an explicit allowlist rather than full os.environ passthrough) is actually a positive security practice that limits credential/secret leakage to child processes. No hardcoded secrets, no command injection (subprocess uses list-form args without shell=True), no eval/exec of untrusted input, and no prompt injection instructions were found in SKILL.md or reference files. The main legitimate concerns are: (1) lack of explicit user disclosure that prompt content is sent to three different third-party AI providers (OpenRouter/Google/Perplexity), which matters for confidential/sensitive infographic content, and (2) references to seemingly fictional/unverifiable model names ('Gemini 3.6 Flash', 'Nano Banana Pro') which could indicate either forward-looking naming or documentation inaccuracy. Several referenced files (assets/*.md, templates/*.md) are missing, which is a completeness issue rather than a security threat since the fallback references/*.md files that do exist are benign, informative content with no embedded instructions or injection attempts. Overall, this skill presents LOW-to-MEDIUM risk, primarily around data-handling transparency rather than any malicious functionality.
llm_primary_threats: Third-party data transmission without explicit disclosure
Documentation/capability naming inconsistency (unverifiable model names)
Missing referenced files (completeness gap, not a security threat)

findings.title: Description references non-existent/fictional AI models ('Nano Banana Pro', 'Gemini 3.6 Flash')
findings.description: The SKILL.md description and body repeatedly reference 'Nano Banana Pro AI' and 'Gemini 3.6 Flash' as the underlying models. As of current knowledge, 'Gemini 3.6' does not correspond to any publicly known Google model version, and 'Nano Banana Pro' appears to be a codename/marketing term rather than a verifiable model. The actual model string used in code is 'google/gemini-3.6-flash' via OpenRouter, which may not resolve to a real, existing model on the OpenRouter platform, potentially causing runtime failures or confusion about what model is actually processing user data. This inflates confidence in the tool's capabilities with specific-sounding but unverifiable model names.
findings.snippet:
self.image_model = "google/gemini-3.6-flash"
self.review_model = "google/gemini-3.6-flash"
findings.remediation: Verify the actual model identifiers available on OpenRouter and update documentation/code to reference real, current model names to avoid confusion or broken functionality.

findings.title: Broad 'allowed-tools' declaration (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) relative to skill's stated scope
findings.description: The manifest declares allowed-tools: Read Write Edit Bash. The scripts do use subprocess (Bash-adjacent) invocation and file writes, which is consistent with declared tools. This is not a violation, but the Bash tool combined with subprocess.run and building a command list from user-controllable arguments (though passed as a list, not shell string) should be noted for completeness; no injection risk was found since subprocess.run uses list-form arguments (not shell=True), which avoids shell injection.
findings.snippet: cmd = [sys.executable, str(ai_script), args.prompt, "-o", args.output] ... result = subprocess.run(cmd, check=False, env=build_subprocess_env(api_key))
findings.remediation: No action required; subprocess is invoked safely without shell=True. Continue avoiding shell string concatenation for command execution.

findings.title: User-provided infographic content sent to multiple third-party AI services without explicit data-handling disclosure
findings.description: The skill sends the user's full infographic prompt (which may contain sensitive business data, unreleased product info, financial figures, personal data for resumes, etc.) to multiple external third-party services: OpenRouter (as a proxy), Google's Gemini model, and Perplexity Sonar Pro (for research). Additionally, when --research is used, the raw topic string is sent to Perplexity for web search, and results are saved to disk in a research JSON file. While this is core, documented functionality of the skill, the SKILL.md does not clearly warn users that their infographic content, potentially including confidential business data, will be transmitted to and processed by three different third-party AI providers. This is a data exposure risk for confidential/sensitive infographic topics (e.g., internal financials, personal health info, unreleased product data).
findings.snippet:
research_model = "perplexity/sonar-pro" ... payload = {"model": research_model, "messages": messages, ...}
self.image_model = "google/gemini-3.6-flash"
findings.remediation: Add explicit disclosure in SKILL.md about which third-party services process user content, and recommend against using confidential/sensitive data with --research or standard generation without reviewing the vendor's data retention policies.

findings.title: API key usage sent to third-party OpenRouter service (expected behavior, not exfiltration)
findings.description: The static analyzer flagged 'environment variable access with network calls' and 'cross-file env var exfiltration' because the OPENROUTER_API_KEY environment variable is read and used in Authorization headers sent to the OpenRouter API (https://openrouter.ai/api/v1). Upon manual review, this is the intended, documented behavior of the skill: the API key is required to call the image-generation and quality-review models via OpenRouter, and there is no evidence of the key or user data being sent to any other undisclosed destination. The subprocess launcher (generate_infographic.py) explicitly minimizes environment forwarding (FORWARDED_ENV_VARS allowlist) rather than passing the full parent environment, which is a good security practice that reduces exposure of unrelated secrets. This is flagged as LOW/informational rather than a true exfiltration since the API key transmission to its own API provider is necessary and expected functionality, not an unauthorized destination.
findings.snippet:
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}", ...}
response = requests.post(f"{self.base_url}/chat/completions", headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=120)
findings.remediation: Document clearly in SKILL.md that user prompts/content (and any research topic text) are sent to third-party APIs (OpenRouter, underlying Google/Perplexity model providers) for processing. Consider allowing users to opt out of --research to avoid sending topic data to Perplexity Sonar, and add a note that generated content and prompts leave the local machine.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-engineered, defensively-designed Agent Skill for organizing ISO 13485 / FDA QMSR / MDSAP / EU MDR-IVDR quality-management evidence. The skill is explicitly and repeatedly self-limiting: SKILL.md states a 'non-negotiable boundary' disclaiming certification, compliance, or legal-applicability determinations, and instructs the agent to always label output as draft material for human review. All bundled Python scripts (_common.py, validate_scope_intake.py, audit_document_records.py, check_capa.py, check_traceability.py, check_qmsr_transition.py, validate_evidence_manifest.py, check_supplier_controls.py, gap_analyzer.py) are pure standard-library JSON/Markdown structural validators with no network calls, no eval/exec, no shell=True subprocess use, no credential access, and explicit safeguards against path traversal (relative_to/resolve/strict checks), symlink inputs, duplicate JSON keys, oversized inputs, non-finite numbers, and unauthorized output overwrite (fail-closed unless --force). The test suite (tests/test_scripts.py) invokes the CLIs safely via subprocess.run with a fixed argv list (no shell=True), which is standard practice and not evidence of true eval/exec risk despite the static analyzer flag on the markdown code block. All referenced files that exist are internal, bundled resources (templates, references) consistent with normal self-contained skill packaging; several referenced paths listed in the manifest do not exist on disk, but these appear to be redundant/alias file lists documented in the instructions rather than externally-sourced or malicious content — no external network URLs are fetched or followed as instructions, and any URLs present (ISO, FDA, EUR-Lex, NANDO, MDCG) are cited as human-reference documentation only, never fetched or executed by the skill. No prompt injection, jailbreak, credential exfiltration, hardcoded secrets, or capability-inflation abuse was found. Findings below are LOW severity and largely informational/precautionary.

findings.title: Broad description with multiple regulatory keywords could increase unwarranted activation
findings.description: The skill description references ISO 13485, FDA QMSR, MDSAP, and EU MDR/IVDR simultaneously, which could cause the skill to be invoked for a wide range of regulatory-adjacent queries. However, the description also explicitly disclaims legal/compliance/certification determinations, which mitigates over-claiming concerns. This is a minor, informational finding rather than a genuine capability-inflation threat.
findings.snippet: description: Prepare and structurally review ISO 13485 QMS scope... Use for ISO 13485 certification-readiness documentation or for separating related FDA QMSR, MDSAP, and EU MDR/IVDR evidence boundaries; not for legal applicability, compliance, or certification decisions.
findings.remediation: No action required; description already includes strong scope-limiting language.

findings.title: allowed-tools includes Bash but only Python interpreter invocation is documented
findings.description: The manifest declares allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Glob], and the instructions consistently invoke scripts via 'python3 scripts/<name>.py' (an interpreter invocation, which typically maps to the Bash tool executing a python3 command, or could be seen as using Bash to launch Python). This is consistent usage, not a violation, but is noted because 'Python' is not listed as an allowed tool despite compatibility notes describing Python 3.11+. This is a minor manifest/behavior consistency observation rather than a real violation, since Bash is present and used to invoke python3.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Read, Write, Bash, Glob / compatibility: Python 3.11+; bundled CLIs use only the standard library...
findings.remediation: Consider adding 'Python' to allowed-tools for clarity, or clarify that Bash is used solely to invoke the python3 interpreter.

findings.title: Static analyzer false-positive: no eval/exec found in reviewed code
findings.description: The pre-scan static analyzer flagged 'MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC' suggesting a Python code block uses eval/exec. Manual review of all provided script files (validate_evidence_manifest.py, audit_document_records.py, check_traceability.py, check_supplier_controls.py, _common.py, gap_analyzer.py, check_qmsr_transition.py, validate_scope_intake.py, check_capa.py, _catalog.py, tests/test_scripts.py) shows no eval, exec, os.system, subprocess with shell=True, or dynamic code execution outside of the test harness's use of subprocess.run to invoke the CLI scripts themselves (a standard, bounded, non-shell test pattern). The CLI scripts explicitly state 'no dynamic evaluation, executable deserialization, pickle, or shell execution' and this claim is consistent with the code. This finding is recorded for completeness given the pre-scan flag, but represents a likely false positive.
findings.snippet: subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(SCRIPTS / script), *arguments], cwd=str(cwd or ROOT), env=env, text=True, capture_output=True, check=False, timeout=10)
findings.remediation: No remediation needed; subprocess.run without shell=True and with a fixed argv list is a safe invocation pattern. Confirm analyzer tuning to reduce false positives on test harnesses.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill package is a well-engineered, defensively coded integration guide and toolset for the official LabArchives ELN and Inventory APIs. The instructions explicitly emphasize verifying official documentation, using HTTPS-only communication, avoiding credential leakage (never logging secrets, signatures, or query strings), validating regional API URLs against an allowlist, and treating notebook content (XML/JSON/attachments) as untrusted data that must never be treated as instructions -- this is a positive security practice reducing indirect prompt injection risk from returned API content. The bundled Python scripts (setup_config.py, entry_operations.py, notebook_operations.py) are network-free (setup_config.py and entry_operations.py explicitly perform no HTTP requests; they only validate inputs, check environment variable presence, and produce redacted signing plans/fingerprints), use only named environment variables (no .env file reading), never print full credentials (only truncated SHA-256 fingerprints), enforce HTTPS-only and allowlisted regional API URLs, and validate untrusted ZIP archive content (notebook_operations.py) with defenses against zip-slip path traversal, symlinks, XXE/DTD entity injection, decompression bombs, and encrypted-member evasion. No hardcoded live secrets were found (only a publicly documented official HMAC test vector used for self-testing). No prompt injection, jailbreak, or instruction-override attempts were found in the SKILL.md body; instead it contains explicit anti-prompt-injection guidance for handling untrusted notebook content. No unauthorized network calls, credential exfiltration, command injection, or obfuscated payloads were identified. The two minor findings are informational/best-practice items rather than active threats.

findings.title: getpass-prompted secret handled in memory (minor exposure surface)
findings.description: The scripts use getpass to prompt for the Access Password when missing from environment variables. While not saved or printed, this introduces an interactive credential-entry path that could be misused if the underlying agent transcript captures terminal input/output, though the code specifically avoids printing values.
findings.snippet: access_password = getpass.getpass(f"{ENV_ACCESS_PASSWORD}: ")
findings.remediation: Document clearly that interactive prompts should only be used in trusted human-operated terminal sessions, not automated agent pipelines, to avoid inadvertent capture of secrets in logs/transcripts.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, well-documented Agent Skill for the LaminDB bioinformatics data lakehouse platform. The SKILL.md and all reference files (core-concepts, data-management, annotation-validation, ontologies, integrations, setup-deployment) are consistent with the stated purpose, contain no prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, or role-redefinition language, and explicitly bake in strong security guidance (never print/log secrets, use IAM roles/secret managers, validate external data with schemas before registration, pin package versions). No executable script files are bundled (only documentation), so there are no direct code-execution, command-injection, or hardcoded-credential findings. Minor issues include several referenced files (assets/, templates/, and stub .py files) that do not exist in the package - a documentation/packaging inconsistency rather than a security threat - and the routine handling of database/cloud credential environment variables in documented workflows, which is expected for this type of infrastructure skill but slightly increases the attack surface if agent behavior were manipulated elsewhere in a session. No exfiltration, obfuscation, capability inflation, or malicious instruction patterns were identified.

This is optional per spec and thus only a minor/informational finding, but combined with the skill's broad scope (cloud storage, database credentials, ontology downloads, workflow integrations) it would benefit from an explicit allowed-tools declaration to reduce ambiguity about tool scope.

findings.title: Instructions include patterns for connecting to external databases/APIs and reading credentials-adjacent environment variables
findings.description: Several reference files (integrations.md, setup-deployment.md) instruct the agent to construct database connection strings from environment variables (e.g., os.environ['SOURCE_DB_URL'], LAMIN_DB_URL) and to interact with cloud storage credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS). While the skill explicitly instructs not to print/log actual secret values (a good practice), the overall workflow does involve the agent handling credential-bearing environment variables and constructing engine connections to arbitrary external databases/REST APIs. If the agent is manipulated (e.g., via a malicious dataset value or prompt injection elsewhere in a session) it could be induced to echo these values or send them externally, since the mechanism for using them is documented and readily available.
findings.snippet: engine = sa.create_engine(os.environ["SOURCE_DB_URL"]) ... export LAMIN_DB_URL='<set-in-secret-manager>' ... export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<redacted>'
findings.remediation: Continue enforcing the 'never print/log secrets' policy; consider adding automated redaction of any environment variable values that look like connection strings/keys before they can appear in tool outputs or artifact metadata.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill (latchbio-integration) is a well-structured, professionally written documentation/integration skill for the LatchBio bioinformatics SDK. It provides extensive, version-specific guidance for using the Latch Python SDK, CLI, Registry, Nextflow/Snakemake integration, and Latch MCP. The instructions consistently emphasize security best practices: never reading/printing auth tokens (~/.latch/token) or signed URLs, requiring user confirmation before destructive operations (rmr, Registry deletion) and paid/GPU compute launches, using get_secret() only inside tasks and never returning secrets as output, avoiding shell injection by preferring subprocess argument lists with check=True, and pinning dependencies for releases. The single Python script (scripts/inspect_latch_sdk.py) is a safe, local-only introspection tool that explicitly avoids network access and authentication, uses regex-based redaction of memory addresses, and only performs importlib-based inspection — no eval/exec, no credential access, no network calls, no file writes outside stdout. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, hardcoded secrets, data exfiltration, or command injection patterns were found in the SKILL.md body or any of the retrievable reference files. The manifest's allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with actual behavior (editing generated code, running CLI commands). Several referenced files (templates/*, assets/*, latch.py) are listed but not found/provided — this is a packaging completeness issue rather than a demonstrated security threat, and is noted as low severity for documentation hygiene. The static analyzer's eval/exec flag appears to be a false positive triggered by unrelated substrings (e.g., 'execution', 'exec --execution-id') rather than genuine dynamic code execution in the reviewed content. Overall, this skill demonstrates strong security-conscious design and does not exhibit malicious or high-risk behavior.

findings.title: Unpinned/floating pre-release SDK version referenced for Snakemake v2 track
findings.description: The nextflow-snakemake.md reference instructs installing an alpha/pre-release pinned version (latch==2.62.1a2) for the Snakemake v2 tutorial track, and separately notes a generated runtime pin to latch[snakemake]==2.55.0.a6. While the document explicitly warns to treat this as pre-release and validate end-to-end, installing alpha packages from PyPI in a production pipeline context introduces supply-chain risk if that alpha release is ever yanked, altered, or compromised. This is a minor/documentation-level concern given the extensive caveats already present in the text.
findings.snippet: uv pip install "latch==2.62.1a2" ... latch[snakemake]==2.55.0.a6
findings.remediation: When possible, prefer stable releases; if alpha/pre-release pins are required, document a process for verifying package integrity (hashes) before installation, and periodically re-validate the pin is still available and unmodified on PyPI.

findings.title: Static analyzer flagged eval/exec pattern in markdown code blocks (false positive context)
findings.description: The pre-scan static analysis flagged two instances of 'MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC' suggesting eval/exec usage in Python code blocks within the markdown reference files. Manual review of the provided reference file contents (workflow-creation.md, resource-configuration.md, registry.md, ui-and-automation.md, data-management.md, operations-and-debugging.md, verified-workflows.md, latch-mcp.md, nextflow-snakemake.md) did not reveal any use of eval() or exec() in the visible code blocks; the pattern may be triggering on unrelated content (e.g., 'execution', 'exec --execution-id', or similar substrings) rather than actual dynamic code execution. This is flagged as low severity pending clarification, since no genuine dynamic code execution risk was identified in the reviewed content.
findings.snippet: Static finding: MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC: Python code block uses eval/exec (x2) - not corroborated by manual text review, likely a false positive on words like 'execution' or CLI 'exec' command
findings.remediation: Re-run static analysis with stricter regex boundaries to avoid matching substrings like 'exec' inside unrelated words (e.g., 'execution', 'latch exec --execution-id') to reduce false positives.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill (latex-posters) is a well-documented, legitimate LaTeX poster-generation assistant. The instructions are detailed and consistent with the stated purpose (poster layout, design, typography, LaTeX package guidance) and do not contain prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, or hidden malicious instructions. The Python scripts (generate_schematic.py / generate_schematic_ai.py) call the OpenRouter API using an explicitly declared OPENROUTER_API_KEY environment variable to generate AI images — this matches the manifest's declared 'openclaw.envVars' metadata and is not unauthorized/undisclosed data exfiltration. The subprocess environment-forwarding function (FORWARDED_ENV_VARS) is a security-conscious design choice that deliberately minimizes leaked environment variables to only those needed for networking/locale, rather than passing the entire parent environment — this is a positive security practice, not a vulnerability. No hardcoded secrets, no command injection via untrusted input, no credential theft from sensitive paths (~/.ssh, ~/.aws), and no evidence of writing outside the project directory were found. The review_poster.sh script only performs read-only PDF inspection (pdfinfo, pdffonts, pdfimages) with no destructive or networked operations. Overall risk is LOW; findings below are informational/awareness-level rather than indicating actual malicious intent.

findings.snippet: "Support for conference presentations, academic posters, and scientific communication. Includes layout design, color schemes, multi-column formats, figure integration, and poster-specific best practices for visual communication."

findings.title: Unbounded/uncapped external API calls could be invoked repeatedly for many small graphics
findings.description: The workflow encourages generating many small, simple graphics (one per case study, timeline point, etc.) rather than combining them, potentially resulting in numerous sequential calls to the paid OpenRouter API per poster. While iterations are capped at 2 per call, the overall number of separate script invocations is unbounded and could lead to excessive API usage/cost if an agent blindly follows the instructions to split every diagram into many small ones.
findings.snippet: "If you need 3 cases → make 3 separate simple graphics (not one complex graphic)" combined with multiple python scripts/generate_schematic.py invocations chained together in the instructions.
findings.remediation: Add guidance to batch or limit the total number of AI generation calls per poster session to avoid unbounded resource/cost consumption, and consider a global call counter or rate limit in the script.

findings.title: OpenRouter API key transmitted to third-party service

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-constructed, legitimate scientific-computing skill for tandem mass spectrometry analysis using the matchms library. The skill's YAML manifest, instructions, bundled Python CLI script, and all resolvable reference documentation are internally consistent, accurately describe matchms 0.33.1 API behavior, and do not contain prompt injection, credential theft, data exfiltration, command injection, or supply-chain risks. The bundled script (library_search.py) demonstrates strong defensive engineering: it explicitly refuses pickle inputs (mitigating deserialization/code-execution risk), enforces a --max-pairs cap to prevent unbounded compute (DoS) from large all-vs-all comparisons, refuses to overwrite existing output files without --force, pins the exact matchms version (0.33.1) for the uv install command, and validates all CLI arguments before execution. No eval/exec/os.system/subprocess calls, no hardcoded secrets, no network calls to attacker-controlled domains, and no attempts to override agent instructions or safety guidelines were found. A static-analyzer flag ('Python code block uses eval/exec') appears to be a false positive — no actual eval() or exec() call exists anywhere in the script or referenced markdown; this likely stems from documentation text mentioning matchms API method names (e.g., process_spectra, compute_losses) that superficially pattern-match keyword scanners. Minor low-severity observations relate to several referenced template/asset files not being bundled (documentation inconsistency, not a security threat) and reliance on user-side vigilance for avoiding accidental unbounded all-vs-all comparisons in ad-hoc code snippets (already mitigated in the bundled CLI via --max-pairs). Overall, this skill exhibits a low security risk profile.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This MATLAB/Octave skill is exceptionally well-engineered from a security standpoint. Its SKILL.md explicitly enumerates dangerous execution surfaces (eval, evalin, assignin, feval, str2func, system/unix/dos, shell escape, Java/.NET/Python integration, MEX, code generation, MAT file deserialization/loadobj) and instructs the agent to NEVER execute untrusted code, always requiring explicit user approval before any runtime launch. All bundled Python CLI scripts (in scripts/) are deliberately non-executing: they only plan, validate, hash, or inventory — never calling subprocess, network libraries, eval/exec, pickle, or os.environ (enforced by the skill's own AST-based unit tests in tests/test_static.py and tests/test_scripts.py, which explicitly forbid subprocess, socket, requests, urllib, pickle, marshal, ctypes, multiprocessing, eval, exec, compile, and __import__). Path handling uses robust validation: symlink-chain rejection, root-confinement via relative_to checks, suffix allowlists, size bounds, and refusal to overwrite existing files. MAT-file inventory explicitly refuses to load values, refuses scipy.io.loadmat, refuses to follow HDF5 soft/external links, and detects/refuses pickle-signature files disguised as .mat. The command planner for MATLAB/Octave produces argv JSON with executes=false and never invokes a subprocess. No hardcoded secrets, no network calls, no credential harvesting, no data exfiltration patterns were found anywhere in the scripts. The manifest's allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Python) are used appropriately: Bash only to invoke the bounded Python CLIs, Write only for new-file scaffolding with collision refusal. Documentation content that mentions eval/feval/pickle/system is explicitly framing these as forbidden/dangerous patterns rather than promoting their use — this triggered a static analyzer false positive that was investigated and found benign. Overall this is a defensively designed, safety-first skill package with no evidence of prompt injection, data exfiltration, command injection, or capability inflation. Only minor documentation/inventory inconsistencies (stale references to a non-existent templates/ directory) were noted as low-severity housekeeping issues.

findings.title: Loading untrusted ML models (.skops) with trust_model=True by default in examples
findings.description: The skill repeatedly demonstrates calling sc.model_based_label_units(..., repo_id=..., trust_model=True) to download and deserialize pretrained classifier models from Hugging Face. Although the docs include a caveat ('only load models from sources you trust'), the example code sets trust_model=True unconditionally for SpikeInterface/UnitRefine_* repos without any verification step, and an agent following the skill literally would auto-trust and execute/deserialize a downloaded .skops model file. Deserializing untrusted model files is a known vector for arbitrary code execution/tool poisoning if the repo_id is ever hijacked, typo'd, or substituted by a compromised network path (MITM), and the skill provides no hash/signature pinning.
findings.snippet:

    sorting_analyzer=analyzer,
    repo_id="SpikeInterface/UnitRefine_noise_neural_classifier",
    trust_model=True,
)
findings.remediation: Pin exact model revisions/commit hashes for Hugging Face repo_id references, verify checksums before setting trust_model=True, and avoid enabling trust_model=True by default in copy-paste example code; require an explicit user confirmation step before deserializing any third-party model artifact.
